title: Botvinnik against Tal, 1960: a sacrifice the engine doubts
outcomes: Tries each of the five key moments before seeing the move and compares the attempt with the engine's first choice
Labels the knight sacrifice at move 21 sound or practical from the depth-16 and depth-22 numbers, and says what those numbers do not prove
Names the move where the game turned (25.Rxb2) and the capture the engine preferred

steps.text: **Botvinnik (White) against Tal (Black)**, game 6 of the 1960 world championship match, Moscow, 26 March 1960; Tal won. The opening was a King's Indian with White's bishop on g2. You play Black at three moments and White at two, each before seeing the game move, and compare your move with the engine's first choice and with the game. Engine numbers are a rating at a stated depth, not proof.

steps.caption: Moves 1 to 19. Step through; the first decision is at the end.

line.say: White starts with 1.c4; Black replies with a knight.
Black's bishop goes to g7.
Black's e-pawn goes to e5.
White's e-pawn goes to e4.
Black's c-pawn goes to c6.
The queen comes to b6, facing the b2 pawn.
The queen moves to b4, still facing b2.
Black's rooks stand on c4 and c8.
White's king steps to h2. Black to move.
Black plays f5.
The bishop retakes on f5.
White's rook goes to a1. Black to move.

steps.caption: After 21...Nf4: White to move. Engine numbers are from White's side. The engine's first choice at move 21 was Nf6.

line.say: White takes the knight with the g-pawn.
Black retakes with the e-pawn.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the position after 21...Nf4 at least 0.8 of a pawn better for White.
At depth 22 the engine rates the position after 21...Nf4 at least 0.8 of a pawn better for White.

steps.prompt: At depths 16 and 22 the engine rates the position after 21...Nf4 at least 0.8 of a pawn better for White. Using Compensation for material, would you label the sacrifice sound or practical, and what would you need to see to change that label?

steps.caption: After 23.Bd2, the game move. The engine's first choice was 23.a3.

line.say: Black's queen takes the b2 pawn.
White's rook goes to b1, facing the queen.
Black's pawn goes to f3. White to move.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the position after 23.Bd2 as roughly level (within 0.8 of a pawn).

steps.caption: After 25.Rxb2 fxe2 (the game). Engine numbers are from White's side.

line.say: White's rook goes to b3. Black to move.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the position after 25...fxe2 at least 2 pawns better for Black.

steps.caption: 26...Rd4 and the rest of the game, move 27 to move 46.

line.say: The rook goes to d4.
The bishop comes to e5 with check.
Black's rook takes on c1.
Black's rook takes on e1 with check.
The bishop takes the d5 pawn.
Black pushes the d-pawn.
Black is clearly winning; the game ended soon after with White resigning.

steps.text: **Where it was decided.** At depths 16 and 22 the engine rates 21...Nf4 at least 0.8 of a pawn better for White, and at depth 16 it preferred 21...Nf6, so the sacrifice looks practical rather than sound. The game turned at 25.Rxb2; at depth 16 the engine preferred 25.Bxf3. Before capturing, list every capture on the board.

steps.prompt: Which of the five moments (19...f5, 21...Nf4, 23.a3, 25.Bxf3, 26...Rd4) would you have missed in a game of your own, and what would you have had to notice to find it?

sources: Game score, at least 46 moves: Wikipedia, 'World Chess Championship 1960' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Chess_Championship_1960; read 29 Oct 2026 through a fetch tool that returns a summary of the page; it gave game 6, Botvinnik White, result 0-1, ECO E69, the move record without capture marks, and a note on the knight sacrifice at move 21) [S] (two web copies, possibly of one database, not independent)

Game score, full, with capture and check marks: GameKnot annotation page (https://gameknot.com/annotation.pl/a-tal-order?gm=12179; read through the same fetch tool; only the move list and the statement that Botvinnik resigned were used, none of the commentary) [S]
Date and code: 365chess listing of the 1960 match (https://www.365chess.com/tournaments/World_Championship_23th_1960/25597; read: round 6, 26 March 1960, E69, 0-1; no move list on the page) [S]

The two move records are equal after removing capture and check marks, except that GameKnot writes 21.Rba1 where Wikipedia writes 21.Ra1; both are the same move. Every move shown is legal in python-chess; the record is verified to 46...Kd4; the last plies and the resignation were not independently confirmed. The two pages may share an upstream database, so they are agreeing copies, not proven independent [V]
Engine statements: Stockfish 19 lite, single thread, depths 16 and 22 via tools/validate.py and a scan with tools/engine.py; evidence under recorded settings, not proofs [V]
No annotator's commentary was read or copied; all wording is ours. Course design: docs/course-families.md
Core skills used, not re-taught: INI.COMPENSATION (Compensation for material), SAC.TYPES (Types of sacrifice), INI.INITIATIVE (The initiative), LOOP.V2 (Thinking Loop v2: checks, captures, threats)
